fixes.explanation: David says, “…but I am a man of prayer.” People are accusing him, and that's how he describes himself. I think that's a strong thing to be known for, because my own comebacks always come out soggy.
That's not how David describes himself here. The words he uses are “…but I am a man of prayer.” Verse 3 says they surround him with hateful words, and verse 4 is where he calls himself that.

A trial does come up in the very next verse, but the prayer asks for an accuser to stand at his right hand, not a judge. The text says, “let an accuser stand at his right hand.” It's easy to mix those two up when you're moving fast.

The prayer says, “When he is tried, let him be found guilty, and may his prayer be regarded as sin.” Those are both requests, and one of them is about his prayer. I think this part is heavy, and it's okay to sit with that for a second.
Verse 11 says, “May the creditor seize all he owns, and strangers plunder the fruits of his labor.” The prayer goes from his family to his belongings. I think that's a hard verse to read.

The text says the opposite. Verse 12 reads, “May there be no one to extend kindness to him, and no one to favor his fatherless children.” The prayer asks for no favor to be shown to them at all. I think it's a heavy verse.

Verse 16 says, “For he never thought to show kindness…” The prayer gives its reason right there, and it's about kindness that never crossed his mind to show. It's about showing kindness, not receiving it.
That's not the word. The verse says, “For he never thought to show kindness…” The point is what never crossed his mind to do, not what he needed. Kindness is supposed to go out the door, friend.
Close, since kindness is the topic, but the direction is flipped. Verse 16 says, “For he never thought to show kindness…” It's about kindness he never thought to show, not kindness he never got.

Verse 17 says, “The cursing that he loved, may it fall on him; the blessing in which he refused to delight, may it be far from him.” The prayer asks that the cursing he loved fall on him, and that the blessing he refused be far from him. That request lines up with what the man chose.

That's a nice thought, but it's not what the prayer says. Verse 17 asks, “…the blessing in which he refused to delight, may it be far from him.” The prayer asks for the blessing to be far from him. It doesn't ask for a change of heart here.
David doesn't make that case. He says, “For I am poor and needy; my heart is wounded within me.” His reason is his need, not a perfect record.

David says, “I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they shake their heads.” He describes himself as fading away, and he also describes the scorn and the head shaking. That's a rough thing to go through, friend. I think it hurts.

David says the opposite. He promises, “With my mouth I will thank the LORD profusely; I will praise Him in the presence of many.” His praise happens in the presence of many, not where no one can hear. Praising in a quiet corner isn't what he promises.
David says, “With my mouth I will thank the LORD profusely; I will praise Him in the presence of many.” He promises to thank the LORD with his mouth. And he says it will be in the presence of many.

A priest doesn't appear in this psalm at all. David says, “For He stands at the right hand of the needy one…” and the He is the LORD. Earlier the prayer asks for an accuser at the right hand of the other man, and here the LORD stands at the needy one's.
